title: Latency-per-Dollar Public Benchmark — Methodology (Chat + Embeddings)
author: Claire Dubois
body:
## 1. Purpose
This page defines the *published* internal methodology used for Redwood Inference’s “Latency per Dollar” benchmark report.

The methodology is designed to:
- Reflect **real production serving economics** (latency + cost) for common LLM workloads.
- Be **reproducible** across runs and comparable across regions.
- Avoid benchmark-only optimizations by fixing runtime policy to a production-realistic profile.

> Note: Public-facing materials may summarize this. This page is the source of truth for *what we actually ran*.

---

## 2. Scope
**Included workloads**
- Chat completions (streaming)
- Embeddings

**Included deployment mode**
- Redwood Hosted API (production runtime profile + benchmark guardrails)

**Not in scope**
- Fine-tuning, tool calling/function calling, multimodal
- Customer traces or customer prompts (no customer data)
- Cross-provider comparisons in this methodology page (handled in claims guidance)

---

## 3. Definitions (what we measure)
### 3.1 Latency definitions
We record the following latency metrics at the client:
- **TTFT (time to first token)**: time from request send to first streamed token received.
- **E2E latency (end-to-end)**: time from request send to final byte received (i.e., completion fully delivered).
- **ITL (inter-token latency)**: mean gap between streamed tokens after the first token (for streaming chat only).

Unless otherwise stated, **the headline latency used for Latency/$ is p50 E2E latency** for the workload.

We also report **p95 E2E** and **p50 TTFT** as supporting reliability/UX indicators.

### 3.2 Throughput definitions
- **Output throughput (tok/s)**: total output tokens divided by wall-clock time of the measurement window.
- **Goodput**: throughput excluding failed requests (non-2xx or client timeout).

### 3.3 Cost definitions
Cost is computed using:
- Metered token counts (input + output) from the benchmark harness + server response headers.
- **List price** in effect at the time of the run (region-specific if applicable).

We report:
- **Effective cost per 1M output tokens** (chat) or **per 1M input tokens** (embeddings), computed from observed token ratios.

> We do **not** include volume discounts, committed spend discounts, negotiated pricing, or credits. This is critical for comparability.

---

## 4. Benchmark workloads
### 4.1 Workload A — Chat (streaming)
**Endpoint**: Chat Completions (streaming enabled)

**Prompt set**: Redwood Public Chat Prompt Set v1 (see §5)

**Generation settings (fixed)**
- Temperature: 0.2
- Top-p: 1.0
- Frequency penalty: 0.0
- Presence penalty: 0.0
- Stop: none
- Seed: not set (we do not depend on determinism; we measure serving)

**Output length policy**
- Max output tokens: 512
- Target output length distribution (by sampling prompts + fixed “continue” instruction) approximates the percentiles below.

**Target token distributions (Chat)**
The harness samples from a fixed distribution to avoid cherry-picking small prompts.

| Metric | p10 | p50 | p90 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Input tokens (prompt + system) | 220 | 650 | 1,450 |
| Output tokens | 110 | 260 | 480 |

**Why these values?**
- p50 reflects common “assistant reply” sizes in SaaS copilots and support automation.
- p90 covers longer troubleshooting / analysis responses without drifting into extreme long-context.

### 4.2 Workload B — Embeddings
**Endpoint**: Embeddings

**Input set**: Redwood Public Embeddings Text Set v1 (see §5)

**Input length distribution (Embeddings)**
| Metric | p10 | p50 | p90 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Input tokens | 60 | 180 | 620 |

**Notes**
- We do not vary embedding dimensionality by request; it is model-defined.
- Output size affects bandwidth but is not the bottleneck in our typical regions; we still record E2E latency at the client.

---

## 5. Prompt/input datasets (no customer data)
### 5.1 Principles
- **No customer prompts** and no customer-derived traces.
- Prompts are drawn from:
  - permissive-licensed public corpora snippets,
  - synthetic prompts written by Redwood,
  - templated variations to preserve distribution stability.
- We exclude:
  - PII, secrets, credentials, or anything that could be construed as personal data.

### 5.2 Redwood Public Chat Prompt Set v1
Composition (approximate weights):
- 35% product/support Q&A (templated; synthetic)
- 30% developer assistance (code explanation, debugging prompts; synthetic)
- 20% summarization/rewrite (public-domain text excerpts)
- 15% extraction/structuring (synthetic)

All prompts are versioned in the benchmark-lab repository (internal), referenced by dataset hash in artifacts.

### 5.3 Redwood Public Embeddings Text Set v1
Composition:
- 50% short queries (search-like)
- 30% sentence/paragraph snippets
- 20% multi-paragraph chunks

Text sources are public domain / permissive where applicable; synthetic where unclear.

---

## 6. Traffic model (concurrency + arrival)
### 6.1 Why we use a traffic model
Latency is a function of load. We therefore measure under a controlled, production-representative concurrency rather than single-request microbenchmarks.

### 6.2 Concurrency targets
We run each model+region+workload at a fixed target concurrency and also a small sweep to detect nonlinearities.

**Default targets (headline numbers)**
- Chat: **C = 32** concurrent in-flight requests
- Embeddings: **C = 128** concurrent in-flight requests

**Sweep (diagnostic only; not always published)**
- Chat: C ∈ {8, 16, 32, 64}
- Embeddings: C ∈ {32, 64, 128, 256}

### 6.3 Arrival process
- Each worker issues a new request immediately after completing the previous one (closed-loop concurrency).
- Workers are evenly distributed across 4 client processes to reduce local scheduling artifacts.

**Why closed-loop?**
It produces a stable concurrency level and is less sensitive to transient network jitter than open-loop RPS drivers.

---

## 7. Environment + runtime policy (consistency rules)
### 7.1 Regions
Benchmarks are executed *within the target region* using regional runners (same cloud region as the serving cluster) to minimize cross-region network effects.

We record:
- region name
- model id + pinned version
- runtime profile name
- pricing snapshot id

### 7.2 Runtime profile (must be stable)
For the public report runs, we use:
- Continuous batching: **enabled**
- Prefix/KV caching across *requests*: **disabled**
- KV cache within a request: **enabled (default)**
- Quantization: **model-specific fixed profile** (do not change mid-cycle)
- Router: **pinned to a single region** (no cross-region fallback during measurement)

Rationale:
- Cross-request caching can dominate economics in some applications but is highly workload-dependent and easy to game. We exclude it for the baseline.

### 7.3 Guardrails (do not impact production SLOs)
Runs must respect SRE constraints:
- Benchmark traffic is tagged and rate-limited.
- If any of the following triggers occur, the run is paused and SRE is paged:
  - region error rate increases by >0.5% absolute for 5 minutes
  - p95 latency for non-benchmark production routes increases by >10% for 5 minutes
  - GPU saturation sustained >95% on shared pools for 3 minutes

(See capacity window plan for exact run windows and escalation.)

---

## 8. Warmup, measurement windows, and sampling
### 8.1 Warmup policy
For each model+region+workload+concurrency configuration:
1) Warm up for **5 minutes** (requests executed but excluded from stats)
2) Measure for **20 minutes**

Additionally:
- The first **100 requests per worker** are excluded even within the warmup window (to avoid initial connection pool and JIT-like effects).

### 8.2 Replicates
- We run **3 replicates** per configuration on separate capacity windows when possible.
- If replicates differ beyond variance thresholds (see §11), we follow anomaly triage.

### 8.3 Timeouts + retries
- Client timeout: 120s per request
- No application-level retries during measurement (retries can hide tail latency)

Failures are counted and included as a separate “error rate” metric.

---

## 9. Instrumentation (what we log)
For each request we record:
- request id
- timestamps: start, first token (chat), end
- input tokens, output tokens
- HTTP status / error code
- region, model id, model version
- concurrency setting

We also capture per-run aggregates:
- total successful requests
- total failed requests
- total input/output tokens
- p50/p95 TTFT and E2E latency
- throughput (tok/s)

**Data handling**
- Raw logs are stored in internal artifact storage with restricted access.
- Public tables are generated from a sanitized schema that contains no prompt text and no per-request identifiers.

---

## 10. Metric computation (including Latency/$)
### 10.1 Cost per token (effective)
We compute an effective cost per token from measured totals.

**Chat**
- total_cost_usd = (total_input_tokens × price_in_per_token) + (total_output_tokens × price_out_per_token)
- effective_cost_per_output_token = total_cost_usd / total_output_tokens
- effective_cost_per_1M_output_tokens = effective_cost_per_output_token × 1,000,000

**Embeddings**
- total_cost_usd = total_input_tokens × price_embed_per_token
- effective_cost_per_input_token = total_cost_usd / total_input_tokens
- effective_cost_per_1M_input_tokens = effective_cost_per_input_token × 1,000,000

If pricing is a single blended rate, we treat price_in = price_out = blended.

### 10.2 Latency/$ (primary metric)
We define **Latency per Dollar** as cost-weighted median end-to-end latency.

**Chat**
- latency_per_dollar = p50_e2e_latency_ms × effective_cost_per_output_token
  - Units: ms·USD per output token
  - Interpretation: “how many milliseconds of median latency you pay for each generated token”

**Embeddings**
- latency_per_dollar = p50_e2e_latency_ms × effective_cost_per_input_token
  - Units: ms·USD per input token

**Why this definition?**
- It rewards both **lower latency** and **lower cost**.
- It is stable under our fixed workload distribution.
- It discourages “cheap but slow” and “fast but expensive” extremes by capturing the joint tradeoff.

> Reporting note: Public charts may scale this value for readability (e.g., ms·USD per 1K tokens). Scaling must be explicit in axis labels.

### 10.3 Supporting metrics (always computed)
- p50 E2E latency (ms)
- p95 E2E latency (ms)
- p50 TTFT (ms) (chat)
- output throughput (tok/s) (chat)
- embedding throughput (req/s and tokens/s) (embeddings)
- error rate (%)

---

## 11. Variance + confidence (how we decide results are stable)
### 11.1 Acceptance thresholds (per configuration)
A configuration is considered stable if:
- p50 E2E replicate CoV (coefficient of variation) ≤ 7%
- p95 E2E replicate CoV ≤ 12%
- error rate ≤ 0.2% (unless a known incident is annotated)

If thresholds are exceeded:
- rerun once in the next capacity window
- if still exceeded, open anomaly triage and require Perf/Evals sign-off before publication

### 11.2 Confidence intervals (reporting guidance)
- We compute bootstrap 95% CIs over per-request samples within each replicate.
- Public report should prefer:
  - “directionally better” language when CIs overlap,
  - explicit “within variance” callouts when appropriate.

---

## 12. Interpreting results (what Latency/$ does and does not say)
### 12.1 What you can conclude
- For the defined workload, in the defined region, at the defined concurrency:
  - which model/runtime configuration delivers better *combined* cost+latency economics.
- How economics change across regions under the same harness.

### 12.2 What you should not conclude
- “Model X is always cheaper” (pricing and token ratios vary by workload).
- “Model X is always faster” (latency depends on context length, output length, and concurrency).
- “These results predict your exact application latency” (your traffic pattern and caching opportunities may differ).

### 12.3 Common pitfalls
- **Comparing results across different workload definitions.** Only compare within the same workload version.
- **Ignoring tail latency.** p50 can look great while p95 regresses under load.
- **Assuming network is irrelevant.** We minimize it by in-region runners, but it’s still part of E2E.

---

## 13. Change control (versioning + refresh cadence)
### 13.1 Versioned inputs
Every published run must pin:
- dataset version/hash
- harness version (benchmark-lab git SHA)
- model version
- runtime profile version
- pricing snapshot id

### 13.2 When we update the methodology
Methodology changes require:
- Approval from Methodology Sponsor (Jonas Weber)
- Review from Stats (Sana Farid) if sampling/CI changes
- Review from Legal (Michael Grant) if public claims are affected
- A new methodology version number (v1, v1.1, v2…)

---

## 14. Appendix A — Practical reproduction guidance (internal)
To reproduce a run internally:
1) Reserve capacity window (per SRE plan)
2) Deploy the pinned harness version
3) Verify runtime profile flags and that cross-request caching is disabled
4) Run warmup + measurement windows
5) Validate:
   - token counts non-zero and sane
   - error rate under threshold
   - replicate variance within thresholds
6) Generate sanitized table artifacts using the public-table build pipeline

---

## 15. Appendix B — Methodology version history
- **v1.0 (2025-01-09):** Initial publication. Defined workloads, distributions, concurrency targets, and Latency/$ computation.
- **v1.1 (2025-02-20):** Clarified Latency/$ units and scaling guidance; tightened variance thresholds; documented closed-loop arrival model explicitly.
